scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire research letter (Liu-Galvin et al., J Am Board Fam Med 2025) is about lost labor costs associated with Long COVID (LC) using 2022 MEPS data; Lyme disease is not mentioned anywhere in the document.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed research letter estimating the 2022 US lost-labor (productivity) costs tied to Long COVID, using nationally representative Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) data on full-time workers. It compares self-reported missed workdays and wages across three groups: never had COVID-19, had COVID-19 without Long COVID, and had Long COVID (defined as COVID-19 symptoms lasting 3+ months). The authors report that individuals with Long COVID had more than twice the mean lost-labor cost of those who never had COVID-19, and they extrapolate this to a national population-level estimate of over $12 billion in lost labor costs in 2022. The study used the human-capital approach (hours × wage × missed days) and does not address direct medical costs, non-medical costs, caregiving burden, or long-term financial consequences.

contextual_issues: The paper notes Long COVID's clinical sequelae are 'quite varied,' but does not quantify specific symptom categories, diagnostic delay, or repeated care-seeking.

Direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help), and caregiving time are referenced only indirectly by citing other studies on LC morbidity/mortality/health care costs (refs 7-9), not quantified in this document itself.

The discussion notes 'most of these costs were likely borne by employers' given high paid-sick-leave prevalence, but this is an inference, not a direct measurement of employer vs. employee cost split.

The paper references a prior modeling study (Bartsch et al.) estimating $1.99–$6.49 billion in employer productivity losses from LC as of early 2024, used only as a discussion comparison, not adopted as this paper's own estimate.
evidence_gaps: No data on direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help), or caregiving time for Long COVID patients or their families.
No measure of diagnostic delay, repeated care-seeking, or insurance/access barriers beyond the single paid-sick-leave analysis.
No lifetime or multi-year cost projection; the estimate is a single calendar-year (2022) snapshot of missed-workday costs only.
No breakdown of lost labor costs by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or other subgroups.
Reliance on self-reported COVID-19/LC history and self-reported missed workdays, with no direct measure of workdays missed specifically attributable to LC versus other causes.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the weighted MEPS sample-level total costs (e.g., $15,863,994,281 for the LC group) with the national population-level extrapolated estimate ($12,784,168,675.20) — these are different quantities: one is a weighted survey-sample total, the other is a BLS-workforce-scaled incremental estimate.

The document's own Table 1 lists an identical total cost figure ($15,863,994,281, SE $1,748,160,632) for both the 'Never had COVID-19' row and the 'Had long COVID' row, while the narrative Results text states different totals for each group ($31,016,098,164 for never-had-COVID-19; $15,863,994,281 for LC; $77,051,513,328 for had-COVID-without-LC). This inconsistency between table and text is preserved here rather than resolved; downstream simulation should flag it rather than silently pick one value.

The population-level estimate uses the BLS count of 131,960,000 full-time workers nationally in 2022, a different population size than the MEPS weighted sample of 104,889,622 — these two population denominators must not be conflated.

This paper's $12.78 billion 2022 estimate is a real-world, self-reported-missed-workday figure using the human-capital approach; the $1.99–$6.49 billion figure from the cited Bartsch et al. modeling study (as of early 2024) uses a different method, population, and time window and must not be pooled or averaged with this paper's estimate — the paper itself only contrasts them in discussion, it does not combine them.

All dollar figures are 2022 USD based on self-reported hourly wage and missed workdays; they reflect only lost-labor/productivity cost from missed workdays due to illness/injury, not a comprehensive cost-of-illness figure (no direct medical, non-medical, or presenteeism costs included).

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: Population-level lost labor cost attributable to Long COVID in 2022 ($12,784,168,675.20) and the per-group mean/median lost labor costs (e.g., $1,944.46 mean for LC) are presented as single pooled national figures with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or other subgroup categories; the document does not state that subgroup variation was checked and found negligible.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document states that there are currently no effective treatments for Long COVID, leaving vaccination as 'the best available strategy' for prevention and framing accelerated research into therapies as an unmet need.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Discussion, p.3 (942-943): 'In the absence of effective treatments, these consequences underscore the need to prioritize prevention through vaccination — the best available strategy to reduce the risk of LC — and accelerate research into effective therapies.'

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire research letter (Liu-Galvin et al., J Am Board Fam Med 2025) is about lost labor costs associated with Long COVID (LC) using 2022 MEPS data; Lyme disease is not mentioned anywhere in the document.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed research letter estimating the 2022 US lost-labor (productivity) costs tied to Long COVID, using nationally representative Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) data on full-time workers. It compares self-reported missed workdays and wages across three groups: never had COVID-19, had COVID-19 without Long COVID, and had Long COVID (defined as COVID-19 symptoms lasting 3+ months). The authors report that individuals with Long COVID had more than twice the mean lost-labor cost of those who never had COVID-19, and they extrapolate this to a national population-level estimate of over $12 billion in lost labor costs in 2022. The study used the human-capital approach (hours × wage × missed days) and does not address direct medical costs, non-medical costs, caregiving burden, or long-term financial consequences.

contextual_issues: The paper notes Long COVID's clinical sequelae are 'quite varied,' but does not quantify specific symptom categories, diagnostic delay, or repeated care-seeking.

Direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help), and caregiving time are referenced only indirectly by citing other studies on LC morbidity/mortality/health care costs (refs 7-9), not quantified in this document itself.

The discussion notes 'most of these costs were likely borne by employers' given high paid-sick-leave prevalence, but this is an inference, not a direct measurement of employer vs. employee cost split.

The paper references a prior modeling study (Bartsch et al.) estimating $1.99–$6.49 billion in employer productivity losses from LC as of early 2024, used only as a discussion comparison, not adopted as this paper's own estimate.
evidence_gaps: No data on direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help), or caregiving time for Long COVID patients or their families.
No measure of diagnostic delay, repeated care-seeking, or insurance/access barriers beyond the single paid-sick-leave analysis.
No lifetime or multi-year cost projection; the estimate is a single calendar-year (2022) snapshot of missed-workday costs only.
No breakdown of lost labor costs by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or other subgroups.
Reliance on self-reported COVID-19/LC history and self-reported missed workdays, with no direct measure of workdays missed specifically attributable to LC versus other causes.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the weighted MEPS sample-level total costs (e.g., $15,863,994,281 for the LC group) with the national population-level extrapolated estimate ($12,784,168,675.20) — these are different quantities: one is a weighted survey-sample total, the other is a BLS-workforce-scaled incremental estimate.

The document's own Table 1 lists an identical total cost figure ($15,863,994,281, SE $1,748,160,632) for both the 'Never had COVID-19' row and the 'Had long COVID' row, while the narrative Results text states different totals for each group ($31,016,098,164 for never-had-COVID-19; $15,863,994,281 for LC; $77,051,513,328 for had-COVID-without-LC). This inconsistency between table and text is preserved here rather than resolved; downstream simulation should flag it rather than silently pick one value.

The population-level estimate uses the BLS count of 131,960,000 full-time workers nationally in 2022, a different population size than the MEPS weighted sample of 104,889,622 — these two population denominators must not be conflated.

This paper's $12.78 billion 2022 estimate is a real-world, self-reported-missed-workday figure using the human-capital approach; the $1.99–$6.49 billion figure from the cited Bartsch et al. modeling study (as of early 2024) uses a different method, population, and time window and must not be pooled or averaged with this paper's estimate — the paper itself only contrasts them in discussion, it does not combine them.

All dollar figures are 2022 USD based on self-reported hourly wage and missed workdays; they reflect only lost-labor/productivity cost from missed workdays due to illness/injury, not a comprehensive cost-of-illness figure (no direct medical, non-medical, or presenteeism costs included).

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: Population-level lost labor cost attributable to Long COVID in 2022 ($12,784,168,675.20) and the per-group mean/median lost labor costs (e.g., $1,944.46 mean for LC) are presented as single pooled national figures with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or other subgroup categories; the document does not state that subgroup variation was checked and found negligible.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document states that there are currently no effective treatments for Long COVID, leaving vaccination as 'the best available strategy' for prevention and framing accelerated research into therapies as an unmet need.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Discussion, p.3 (942-943): 'In the absence of effective treatments, these consequences underscore the need to prioritize prevention through vaccination — the best available strategy to reduce the risk of LC — and accelerate research into effective therapies.'

spec.title: 2022 Long COVID Lost-Labor (Productivity) Cost Simulator
spec.boundary: This simulation covers only lost-labor/productivity costs (missed workdays x wages, the human-capital approach) for US full-time workers in 2022, as reported in a single research letter using MEPS survey data. It does not include direct medical costs, non-medical costs (travel, paid help), caregiving time, multi-year/lifetime costs, or subgroup breakdowns by sex, age, or race/ethnicity. Associations shown are observational; the study did not test whether earlier diagnosis or treatment changes these costs.

takeaway.patient: A 2022 US study of full-time workers using a national government survey (MEPS) found that people who reported Long COVID (COVID-19 symptoms lasting 3 months or more) had, on average, about $1,242 per year more in lost-labor cost (the value of missed workdays, based on wages) than people who never had COVID-19, and about $479 per year more than people who had COVID-19 but did not develop Long COVID - this smaller difference only barely met the study's own statistical threshold for significance. These are group averages for this study's sample of full-time workers, not a prediction for any one person, and this measure covers missed-workday cost only, not medical bills or other expenses. The study also found paid sick leave was about as common among people with Long COVID (about 80 percent) as in the overall sample (about 81 percent), and the mathematical link between having paid sick leave and having Long COVID did not reach statistical significance.
takeaway.care: This 2022 national survey-based estimate shows full-time workers with Long COVID had a mean lost-labor cost about $1,242/year higher than workers who never had COVID-19, and about $479/year higher than workers who had COVID-19 without Long COVID - the latter comparison only barely crossed the study's own significance threshold (p=0.0485), so it should be treated as a modest, not dramatic, distinction between these two groups. Paid sick leave availability did not differ significantly between the Long COVID group and the overall sample in this data. The figures reflect self-reported missed workdays and wages only, not a clinical severity measure or a diagnostic tool.
takeaway.policy: Scaling the mean lost-labor cost difference between Long COVID and never-had-COVID-19 workers to the full 2022 US full-time workforce using the study's own formula and reported Long COVID prevalence (7.8 percent of the study sample) yields a national estimate of roughly $12.8 billion in lost-labor costs in 2022. This is a missed-workday productivity estimate only, not a comprehensive cost-of-illness figure, and is a different quantity from the weighted MEPS sample-level totals also reported in the source. The study found no statistically significant association between paid sick leave availability and Long COVID status (odds ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.66-1.23, p=0.51), so this should not be cited as evidence that sick leave access differs by Long COVID status.

patient: If you are missing workdays due to long-term COVID-19 symptoms, these study figures may help you describe the general scale of a typical lost-income impact when discussing options with an employer or a disability-benefits program, while keeping in mind your own situation may differ substantially from this average.

If you are unsure whether paid sick leave applies to your circumstances, consider asking your employer or HR directly about the specific policy, since this study only measured whether leave existed, not how it was used.
Keep in mind this study did not measure medical bills, travel costs, or caregiving time, so these numbers reflect only part of the overall financial picture of Long COVID.
care: Consider referencing these national lost-workday cost patterns as general context in return-to-work or workload-accommodation conversations with patients reporting Long COVID, while being clear these are survey-sample group averages, not individualized predictions.

When documenting work-capacity impacts for leave or disability paperwork, note that the mean cost difference between Long COVID and COVID-without-LC patients in this study only barely reached statistical significance (p=0.0485) - this may be worth keeping in mind as a modest rather than dramatic distinction.

This study's finding that paid sick leave availability did not differ significantly for Long COVID patients may be worth checking against patterns observed in your own patient population before assuming otherwise.
policy: Use the population-level 2022 lost-labor cost estimate to inform workforce/economic-impact discussions of Long COVID, scoping it explicitly to missed-workday productivity cost rather than total cost of illness, since medical, non-medical, and caregiving costs are not included.

When evaluating paid-sick-leave policy, treat the paid-sick-leave/Long-COVID association in this study (odds ratio 0.90, p=0.51) as inconclusive rather than citing it as evidence that leave access is or is not affected by Long COVID status.

If modeling alternative workforce-size or prevalence assumptions, recompute the national estimate using this tool's population-level output rather than substituting the weighted MEPS sample-level total, since the source treats these as different quantities.

Consider this productivity-cost estimate alongside the source document's own discussion point that no proven Long COVID treatments currently exist and that vaccination is described as the best available prevention strategy, when weighing research or prevention investment priorities.

outputs.label: Mean lost-labor cost gap: Long COVID minus never-had-COVID-19 (positive = Long COVID group higher)

A larger value means a bigger reported gap in missed-workday cost between these two groups; given the input ranges used here, this value stays positive, consistent with the document's reported ordering.

outputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported 2022 mean lost-labor cost difference between full-time workers who had COVID-19 without Long COVID and those who never had COVID-19, also reported as statistically significant. A larger value means a bigger gap attributable to having had COVID-19 at all, separate from the additional Long COVID effect shown in the next output.

outputs.label: Mean lost-labor cost gap: Long COVID minus had-COVID-19-without-LC (positive = Long COVID group higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported 2022 mean lost-labor cost difference specifically attributable to developing Long COVID versus having COVID-19 without lasting symptoms. The document reports this difference only barely reached its own significance threshold (p=0.0485), so it should be read as a modest, borderline distinction rather than a strong one.

outputs.label: National 2022 lost-labor cost attributable to Long COVID (population-scaled)
outputs.interpretation: This reproduces the document's own extrapolation formula exactly: the mean cost gap between Long COVID and never-had-COVID-19 workers, multiplied by the national full-time workforce count and the study's reported Long COVID prevalence share. With the default inputs this matches the document's own stated figure of approximately $12.78 billion for 2022. This is a different quantity from the weighted MEPS sample-level totals also reported in the source and should not be combined with them; it reflects missed-workday productivity cost only, not total cost of illness.

outputs.label: Paid sick leave prevalence gap: overall sample minus Long COVID group (positive = overall sample higher, negative = Long COVID group higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is the difference between the overall study sample's paid-sick-leave rate and the Long COVID group's rate. The document's own regression analysis found the association between paid sick leave and Long COVID status did not reach statistical significance (odds ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.66-1.23, p=0.51), so this gap should not be read as evidence of a real difference in leave access, regardless of its sign or size.

package.documentation:
## Source
This simulator is built from Liu-Galvin et al., *Journal of the American Board of Family Medicine* 2025;38:941-943, a research letter estimating 2022 US lost-labor (productivity) costs associated with Long COVID using Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) data on full-time workers, with a human-capital approach (hours x wage x missed workdays).

## Scope
All dollar figures are 2022 USD reflecting only lost-labor/productivity cost from self-reported missed workdays due to illness or injury. The document does not quantify direct medical costs, non-medical costs (travel, paid help), caregiving time, or multi-year financial consequences, and this simulator does not add any of those.

## Parameters
Mean lost-labor costs per person for the never-had-COVID-19, had-COVID-19-without-Long-COVID, and Long COVID groups are taken directly from the document's Table 1 and Results text. Their exploration ranges were deliberately narrowed and kept non-overlapping so that sliders or sensitivity exploration cannot reverse the document's reported group ordering (Long COVID highest, then COVID-without-LC, then never-had-COVID-19). The national full-time workforce count (BLS, 2022) and the study-sample Long COVID prevalence (7.8%) are the same two scaling factors the document itself used to produce its national estimate; multiplying the Long-COVID-vs-never-had-COVID-19 cost gap by these two factors reproduces the document's own stated ~$12.78 billion 2022 national estimate.

## Known inconsistency in the source
The document's own Table 1 lists an identical total weighted cost figure for both the never-had-COVID-19 and Long COVID rows, while its narrative text states different totals for each group. This inconsistency is noted here rather than resolved, and this simulator avoids using those ambiguous weighted-sample totals, relying instead on the mean per-person costs and the document's separately stated national-scaling formula.

## Limitations
The pooled national and per-group cost figures have not been checked by the source for variation by sex, age, or race/ethnicity; federal survey data such as NHIS and BRFSS generally support such disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform one. The document also notes, in its discussion, that no proven treatments for Long COVID currently exist, framing vaccination as the best available prevention strategy and accelerated treatment research as an unmet need - a limitation of the evidence/treatment landscape itself, distinct from the accuracy of the cost estimates above. All associations describe patterns the study observed in survey data; the document did not test whether earlier diagnosis or treatment changes these costs.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Population-level lost labor cost attributable to Long COVID in 2022: 12,784,168,675 in 2022 dollars is about 14,063,568,419 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.100). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Total estimated lost labor cost for individuals with Long COVID (weighted MEPS sample): 15,863,994,281 in 2022 dollars is about 17,451,613,370 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.100). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Mean lost labor cost per individual with Long COVID: 1,944.46 in 2022 dollars is about 2,139.06 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.100). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Mean lost labor cost per individual who never had COVID-19: 702.42 in 2022 dollars is about 772.72 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.100). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Mean lost labor cost per individual who had COVID-19 without Long COVID: 1,465.55 in 2022 dollars is about 1,612.22 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.100). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Difference in mean lost labor cost: Long COVID vs never had COVID-19: 1,242.04 in 2022 dollars is about 1,366.34 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.100). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Weighted prevalence of Long COVID in the 2022 MEPS full-time worker study sample (2022): the document reports 7.8% as the share of all U.S. adults that ever experienced Long COVID; the national survey's 7 wave(s) in that period ranged from 14% to 14.8% (interval bounds 13.4% to 15.4%), so the document's figure is below every survey wave interval in that period. The survey is self-reported adults; a different definition or population in the document makes a gap expected, so treat it as a prompt to check. Federal source: household survey (self-report), 2022-2024; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.

spec.title: 2022 Long COVID Lost-Labor (Productivity) Cost Simulator
spec.boundary: This simulation covers only lost-labor/productivity costs (missed workdays x wages, the human-capital approach) for US full-time workers in 2022, as reported in a single research letter using MEPS survey data. It does not include direct medical costs, non-medical costs (travel, paid help), caregiving time, multi-year/lifetime costs, or subgroup breakdowns by sex, age, or race/ethnicity. Associations shown are observational; the study did not test whether earlier diagnosis or treatment changes these costs.

takeaway.patient: A 2022 US study of full-time workers using a national government survey (MEPS) found that people who reported Long COVID (COVID-19 symptoms lasting 3 months or more) had, on average, about $1,242 per year more in lost-labor cost (the value of missed workdays, based on wages) than people who never had COVID-19, and about $479 per year more than people who had COVID-19 but did not develop Long COVID - this smaller difference only barely met the study's own statistical threshold for significance. These are group averages for this study's sample of full-time workers, not a prediction for any one person, and this measure covers missed-workday cost only, not medical bills or other expenses. The study also found paid sick leave was about as common among people with Long COVID (about 80 percent) as in the overall sample (about 81 percent), and the mathematical link between having paid sick leave and having Long COVID did not reach statistical significance.
takeaway.care: This 2022 national survey-based estimate shows full-time workers with Long COVID had a mean lost-labor cost about $1,242/year higher than workers who never had COVID-19, and about $479/year higher than workers who had COVID-19 without Long COVID - the latter comparison only barely crossed the study's own significance threshold (p=0.0485), so it should be treated as a modest, not dramatic, distinction between these two groups. Paid sick leave availability did not differ significantly between the Long COVID group and the overall sample in this data. The figures reflect self-reported missed workdays and wages only, not a clinical severity measure or a diagnostic tool.
takeaway.policy: Scaling the mean lost-labor cost difference between Long COVID and never-had-COVID-19 workers to the full 2022 US full-time workforce using the study's own formula and reported Long COVID prevalence (7.8 percent of the study sample) yields a national estimate of roughly $12.8 billion in lost-labor costs in 2022. This is a missed-workday productivity estimate only, not a comprehensive cost-of-illness figure, and is a different quantity from the weighted MEPS sample-level totals also reported in the source. The study found no statistically significant association between paid sick leave availability and Long COVID status (odds ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.66-1.23, p=0.51), so this should not be cited as evidence that sick leave access differs by Long COVID status.

patient: If you are missing workdays due to long-term COVID-19 symptoms, these study figures may help you describe the general scale of a typical lost-income impact when discussing options with an employer or a disability-benefits program, while keeping in mind your own situation may differ substantially from this average.

If you are unsure whether paid sick leave applies to your circumstances, consider asking your employer or HR directly about the specific policy, since this study only measured whether leave existed, not how it was used.
Keep in mind this study did not measure medical bills, travel costs, or caregiving time, so these numbers reflect only part of the overall financial picture of Long COVID.
care: Consider referencing these national lost-workday cost patterns as general context in return-to-work or workload-accommodation conversations with patients reporting Long COVID, while being clear these are survey-sample group averages, not individualized predictions.

When documenting work-capacity impacts for leave or disability paperwork, note that the mean cost difference between Long COVID and COVID-without-LC patients in this study only barely reached statistical significance (p=0.0485) - this may be worth keeping in mind as a modest rather than dramatic distinction.

This study's finding that paid sick leave availability did not differ significantly for Long COVID patients may be worth checking against patterns observed in your own patient population before assuming otherwise.
policy: Use the population-level 2022 lost-labor cost estimate to inform workforce/economic-impact discussions of Long COVID, scoping it explicitly to missed-workday productivity cost rather than total cost of illness, since medical, non-medical, and caregiving costs are not included.

When evaluating paid-sick-leave policy, treat the paid-sick-leave/Long-COVID association in this study (odds ratio 0.90, p=0.51) as inconclusive rather than citing it as evidence that leave access is or is not affected by Long COVID status.

If modeling alternative workforce-size or prevalence assumptions, recompute the national estimate using this tool's population-level output rather than substituting the weighted MEPS sample-level total, since the source treats these as different quantities.

Consider this productivity-cost estimate alongside the source document's own discussion point that no proven Long COVID treatments currently exist and that vaccination is described as the best available prevention strategy, when weighing research or prevention investment priorities.

inputs.label: Mean lost-labor cost, Long COVID group
inputs.source: Observed value from Results, p.2 and Table 1; the 1800-2500 exploration range is an assumed bound chosen so it cannot overlap with the other two group ranges, preserving the document's own reported group ordering.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported average 2022 lost-labor cost for full-time workers with Long COVID; raising or lowering it changes how large the cost differences and the national estimate below appear, while staying within the range that preserves this group's reported higher-cost position relative to the other two groups.

inputs.label: Mean lost-labor cost, had COVID-19 without Long COVID
inputs.source: Observed value from Table 1 and Results, p.2; the 1150-1750 exploration range is an assumed bound chosen so it cannot overlap with the never-had-COVID-19 or Long COVID ranges.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported average 2022 lost-labor cost for full-time workers who had COVID-19 but not Long COVID; comparing this to the Long COVID value tests how close the two illness-related groups are to each other, which the document reports as only barely statistically significant.

inputs.label: Mean lost-labor cost, never had COVID-19
inputs.source: Observed value from Table 1; the 300-1100 exploration range is an assumed bound chosen so it cannot overlap with the other two group ranges.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported average 2022 lost-labor cost for full-time workers who never had COVID-19, used as the baseline for both cost-difference outputs below; moving it changes the size of both differences but not their direction given the chosen ranges.

inputs.label: US full-time workers, 2022 (BLS count)
inputs.source: Observed value cited in Results, p.2 (BLS full-time workforce count used in the document's own national extrapolation); the 100,000,000-150,000,000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the national full-time workforce size the document used to scale its sample-based cost difference into a national total; increasing it answers 'what if the workforce were larger or smaller' and directly scales the national estimate below.

inputs.label: Long COVID prevalence in study sample
inputs.source: Observed value from Results, p.2 (weighted prevalence among the 2022 MEPS full-time worker study sample, not the general US adult population); the 0-20 range is an assumed exploration bound.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of the study's full-time-worker sample reporting Long COVID, used by the document to scale its per-person cost difference to a national total; a higher value answers 'what if Long COVID were more widespread among full-time workers' and directly raises the national estimate below.

inputs.label: Paid sick leave prevalence, overall study sample
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of the full 2022 MEPS full-time worker study sample reporting paid sick leave; comparing it to the Long COVID group's rate below tests whether leave access looked different for that group in this study.

inputs.label: Paid sick leave prevalence, Long COVID group
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of full-time workers with Long COVID reporting paid sick leave; the document's own regression found no statistically significant association between leave status and Long COVID, so changes here should be read alongside that caveat rather than as evidence of a real difference.

outputs.label: Mean lost-labor cost gap: Long COVID minus never-had-COVID-19 (positive = Long COVID group higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported 2022 mean lost-labor cost difference between full-time workers with Long COVID and those who never had COVID-19; the document reports this specific difference as statistically significant (p<0.0001). A larger value means a bigger reported gap in missed-workday cost between these two groups; given the input ranges used here, this value stays positive, consistent with the document's reported ordering.

outputs.label: Mean lost-labor cost gap: had COVID-19 without Long COVID minus never-had-COVID-19 (positive = COVID-without-LC group higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported 2022 mean lost-labor cost difference between full-time workers who had COVID-19 without Long COVID and those who never had COVID-19, also reported as statistically significant. A larger value means a bigger gap attributable to having had COVID-19 at all, separate from the additional Long COVID effect shown in the next output.

outputs.label: Mean lost-labor cost gap: Long COVID minus had-COVID-19-without-LC (positive = Long COVID group higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported 2022 mean lost-labor cost difference specifically attributable to developing Long COVID versus having COVID-19 without lasting symptoms. The document reports this difference only barely reached its own significance threshold (p=0.0485), so it should be read as a modest, borderline distinction rather than a strong one.

outputs.label: National 2022 lost-labor cost attributable to Long COVID (population-scaled)
outputs.interpretation: This reproduces the document's own extrapolation formula exactly: the mean cost gap between Long COVID and never-had-COVID-19 workers, multiplied by the national full-time workforce count and the study's reported Long COVID prevalence share. With the default inputs this matches the document's own stated figure of approximately $12.78 billion for 2022. This is a different quantity from the weighted MEPS sample-level totals also reported in the source and should not be combined with them; it reflects missed-workday productivity cost only, not total cost of illness.

outputs.label: Paid sick leave prevalence gap: overall sample minus Long COVID group (positive = overall sample higher, negative = Long COVID group higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is the difference between the overall study sample's paid-sick-leave rate and the Long COVID group's rate. The document's own regression analysis found the association between paid sick leave and Long COVID status did not reach statistical significance (odds ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.66-1.23, p=0.51), so this gap should not be read as evidence of a real difference in leave access, regardless of its sign or size.
